Specifically, it forgets the law of thermodynamics, which says that you cannot create or destroy matter. Because of this, a future with no waste, where all material "loops" are closed, and products are recycled forever is, in any practical sense, impossible. They point out that recycling itself uses energy and resources. They also say there is a limit to how many times materials can be recycled before they become low quality. Critics also question if it is even possible ("feasible") to use circular economy ideas all over the world. They say this is because supply chains are very complex and different countries have very different economic and political systems. Furthermore, critics argue that focusing so much on "circularity" might take attention away from other important ways to be sustainable, like simply using less stuff (reducing consumption) and making sure things are fair for everyone (promoting social equity). Also, some critics argue that the circular economy, as it is pushed today, is a 'neoliberal' idea. They say it helps keep the current powerful people in charge and continues unfairness (inequalities). They argue that focusing on "win-win" solutions and making a "business case" for being circular ignores the fact that we might need bigger, more basic changes to our economy and society. Finally, critics point out the risk of "rebound effects". This is when being more efficient (like through circularity) makes things cheaper or easier to get, which causes people to use more of them. This increased use can cancel out the good things the circular economy was supposed to do for the environment. The circular economy seems more sustainable than the usual linear economy. It reduces the use of resources, waste, and pollution. But some experts say this is too simple and ignores the complexity of real systems. For example, social sustainability is often not fully considered. Sometimes, other strategies like buying new energy-efficient equipment are needed. Research from Cambridge and TU Delft identified at least eight ways circular economy relates to sustainability. Innovation is also a key part of development in a circular economy. The circular economy applies to many areas: industries, products, services, and natural resources. Practices and policies help understand current limitations. It also includes strategic management and potential reuse and waste management. The circular economy covers products, buildings, infrastructure, and equipment. It uses both technical (metals, minerals, fossil fuels) and biological resources (food, timber, fibres). Many recommend switching to renewable energy and valuing diversity. Circular economy also involves finance and economic measurements. Modularization can support circular economy and sustainable energy systems. Renting products instead of owning them is another example. Recycling is widespread. Circle Economy reports global circular economy could cut 22.8 billion tons of emissions (39% of 2019 emissions). By 2050, circular economy strategies in cement, aluminum, steel, plastics, and food could reduce almost half of emissions from goods production. In 1966, Kenneth Boulding described a "closed economy" where resources stay longer, compared to an open economy. This is seen as an early form of circular economy. Circular economy is based on feedback and non-linear systems from nature. Concepts like cradle to cradle, industrial ecology, biomimicry, and blue economy influenced it. In 1989, David W. Pearce and R. Kerry Turner noted traditional economies lack recycling and treat environment as a waste sink. In the 1990s, Tim Jackson promoted preventive environmental management and circular approaches. Walter Stahel and Genevieve Reday in 1976 proposed an economy in loops, creating jobs, saving resources, and reducing waste. Stahel promoted longer product life and a service-based economy. China included circular economy in its 11th five-year plan (2006–2010). Ellen MacArthur Foundation popularized the concept. Circular economy helps reduce dependency on cheap oil and supports low-carbon economy. Circular strategies could bridge half of the emissions reduction gap for COP21 1.5°C target. Linear "take, make, dispose" systems use resources and create waste. Circular economy treats systems like living organisms, keeping materials in loops. Walter R. Stahel promoted "Cradle to Cradle" instead of "Cradle to Grave". Steve D. Parker studied closed-loop agricultural systems. Cradle to Cradle design focuses on safe and high-quality products, not just recycling. Architect William McDonough widely implemented this approach. Several circular economy models use steps starting with "R". The original "Three R principle" is "Reduce, Reuse, Recycle" from the 1970s. The most detailed "10R principle" was developed by Jacqueline Cramer. In 2013, a report titled Towards the Circular Economy: Economic and Business Rationale for an Accelerated Transition was released. It was commissioned by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and developed by McKinsey & Company, and it was the first report of its kind. The report looked at the economic and business potential of a circular economy. It uses product case studies and economy-wide analysis, showing benefits across the EU. It estimates that part of the EU manufacturing sector could save up to $630 billion in materials costs by 2025, stimulating areas like product development, remanufacturing, and refurbishment. Key building blocks for circular transition were identified: skills in circular design and production, new business models, skills for cascades and reverse cycles, and cross-sector collaboration. A case study from the automotive industry shows the importance of integrating circular models across product, process, and system levels. A 2015 report by WRAP and Green Alliance, "Employment and the circular economy: job creation in a more resource efficient Britain", examined policy scenarios to 2030. Without policy change, 200,000 jobs may be created, reducing unemployment by 54,000. Aggressive policy could create 500,000 jobs and reduce unemployment by 102,000. The International Labour Organization predicts global circular economy adoption could create 7–8 million additional jobs by 2030. However, circular economy adoption may also cause job losses in emerging economies. In the U.S., Ranta et al. analyzed drivers and barriers for circular economy using Scott's institutional framework. Product-oriented case: Dell—first to offer free recycling and sell computers made from verified recycled materials. Waste management case: Republic Services, second-largest US waste management company. Indicators were categorized as drivers (support circular economy) or barriers (hinder it). On 2 March 2022, representatives from 175 countries pledged to create a legally binding agreement to end plastic pollution by 2024. This includes full lifecycle management of plastics and alternatives like reusability. The agreement is expected to support circular economy and reduce GHG emissions by 25%. The waste sector could achieve net-zero emissions with circular approaches. Circular economy was highlighted at the 2024 COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan also signed a Joint Resolution on global collaboration for efficiency and circularity. Product design for durability, maintenance, repair, upgrade, remanufacturing, separability, disassembly, and reassembly is key for circularity. Standardization supports sustainable advantages for businesses and consumers. Standardization and compatibility improve multi-functionality and modularity. A "Product Family Approach" helps with commonality, compatibility, standardization, or modularization across products. Emerging technologies should be designed with circular principles from the start, including solar panels. Circular process design is crucial for health and sustainability. Much e-waste is recycled far from consumption sites, with low efficiency and negative health effects. Recycling should reduce overall environmental impacts using a life-cycle assessment approach. Mandatory certification for e-waste recyclers could incentivize high-quality processes. Digitalization can improve efficiency and minimize waste. Initially, focus was on re-X technologies (recycling, remanufacturing, reuse), but implementation lagged behind capability. Stakeholder collaboration is key, shifting attention to business-model innovation. Rheaply, a platform for scaling reuse, supports circular business model transition. Circular business models aim to close, narrow, slow, intensify, and dematerialize resource loops, using recycling, efficiency, life extension, and service-based approaches. They are enabled by circular supply chains, collaboration, and innovation. Circular products and models depend on the material affordances for reuse and recovery.Circular business models cannot always be copied from one place to another. Local rules, infrastructure, social norms, and customer expectations can affect how companies use these models. In the textile industry, a circular economy means that clothes and fibers are kept in use for as long as possible. They are reused, repaired, redesigned and recycled so they can re-enter the economy instead of becoming waste. This is different from the current linear model of fashion, where raw materials are taken from nature, turned into products, bought, used, and then thrown away. (Business of Fashion, 2017). ‘Fast fashion’ companies make this problem worse by encouraging people to buy more clothes more often. This “take–make–dispose” model leads to more than $500 billion of economic value lost every year and also has many negative environmental and social impacts (Business of Fashion, 2018). Environmental impacts include huge amounts of clothing going to landfills or being burned. Social impacts include pressure on workers and risks to human rights. The documentary The True Cost (2015) explains that in fast fashion, low wages, unsafe working conditions, and factory disasters are often accepted because they are said to provide jobs for people who have no other options. This shows that fast fashion harms both people and the planet by following a linear system. Many people argue that using a circular economy approach can help make the textile industry more sustainable. A 2017 report by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, "A New Textiles Economy", lists four main goals to move towards a circular textiles system: phase out harmful substances and reduce microfiber release change how clothes are designed, sold, and used so they are not seen as disposable improve recycling by changing how clothes are designed, collected, and processed use resources more efficiently and switch to renewable inputs where possible So far, only a small number of fashion designers and brands have fully taken the lead on circular practices. Some often-cited examples are Patagonia, Eileen Fisher, Nathalia JMag, and Stella McCartney. One example of a circular system within a brand is Eileen Fisher’s “Tiny Factory”. In this program, customers are encouraged to bring back their worn Eileen Fisher clothing so the company can repair, remake, and resell the items instead of throwing them away. There are similar initiatives in Europe, where several outdoor clothing companies run textile return systems that invite customers to bring back used garments for repair, redesign, resale, or recycling. In a 2018 interview, Eileen Fisher said that overconsumption is a major problem in fashion. She argued that brands “need to make less and sell less”. In other words, companies can still use creativity and create value, but should not constantly create more and more new products. Circular business models in fashion also include clothing rental services. These start-ups are growing in both the EU and the US. They offer everyday clothes, maternity wear, and baby clothes for rent, instead of selling them. Some companies, like Palanta, use a “pay as you rent” model, while others, such as Rent The Runway and Le Tote, use monthly subscription models. Both China and Europe are seen as leaders in building a circular economy. McDowall et al. (2017) argue that the Chinese view of the circular economy is broad. It covers pollution and many environmental issues together with resource and waste topics. Europe’s view is usually narrower, focusing more on waste, resource efficiency, and business opportunities. The construction sector is one of the world’s largest waste producers. A circular economy is seen as a useful way to reduce the environmental impact of this industry. Construction is very important for the economy of the European Union (EU) and its member states. It provides around 18 million direct jobs and makes up about 9% of the EU’s gross domestic product (GDP). However, the sector has a large environmental impact because it uses many non-renewable resources and produces a lot of waste. Both of these are increasing quickly. In the EU, people and companies together generate more than 2 billion tonnes of waste every year. This is about 4.8 tonnes per person, mainly from building, mining, and manufacturing. Each person in Europe generates about half a tonne of municipal waste per year, and less than half of that is recycled. Cement production is also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions. It accounts for about 2.4% of global CO2 emissions from industrial and energy sources. Decisions about circular economy practices in construction can be made at different levels: operational level – focused on specific parts of the production process tactical level – focused on whole processes strategic level – focused on the whole company or organization Circular decisions can be made for construction companies themselves, but also for individual construction projects, where the construction company is one of the stakeholders. End-of-life buildings can be deconstructed instead of demolished. This means that buildings are taken apart carefully, so that construction elements can be reused in new buildings. This also frees up land for new development. Modular construction systems can also support a circular economy. Buildings made from modules can be assembled, disassembled, and reused more easily in the future, and their components are usually easier to recover at the end of life. On the operational level, circular approaches can include using reusable or natural materials. For example, crushed and cleaned walnut husks can be used as a hard, light, natural abrasive for cleaning brick surfaces. The abrasive grains from walnut shells can be reused several times. Researchers have also started to measure how well circular economy ideas are being implemented in construction companies. A first attempt created a measurement scale for circular practices in a building company. Studies show that the circular economy in construction can create new jobs and support economic growth. According to Górecki, one possible new job role is a “circular economy manager” for construction projects. This person would be responsible for planning and managing circular strategies across the project. The circular economy is also starting to grow in the automotive industry. A case study in the heavy-duty and off-road industry looks at how circular practices can be added to a lean manufacturing system, which is currently the most common production strategy in the automotive sector. Lean manufacturing improves efficiency by removing waste and focusing on what customers value most. This helps with eco-efficiency by “narrowing” resource loops (using fewer resources for the same output). However, to fully support a circular economy, it is also important to “slow” and “close” resource loops, for example by making products last longer and by reusing and recycling materials. This leads to eco-effectiveness, which looks at the whole system, not just single processes. The study finds that combining lean and circular approaches can unlock large potential benefits by focusing on products, processes, and the overall system at the same time. There are also economic reasons for carmakers to move towards circular models. A 2016 report by Accenture said that circular economy strategies could change how companies compete in the automotive sector in terms of price, quality, and convenience. It suggested that circular practices could double revenues by 2030 and reduce costs by up to 14%. So far, typical actions include: using parts and materials made from recycled content, improving the design of new cars so that they are easier to repair, reuse, and recycle. Remanufacturing is mainly used today for spare parts. A common example is the remanufacturing of gearboxes. A study shows that a remanufactured gearbox can reduce the global warming potential (measured in CO2-equivalent) by about 36% compared to a newly manufactured gearbox. In the EU, the vehicle recycling industry is able to recycle about 75% of each end-of-life vehicle. This means around 25% is not recycled and may end up in landfills. There is therefore still a lot of room to improve circularity in the sector. In the electric vehicle industry, disassembly robots are being developed and used to help take apart vehicles and their battery packs for recycling. The EU’s ETN-Demeter project (European Training Network for the Design and Recycling of Rare-Earth Permanent Magnet Motors and Generators in Hybrid and Full Electric Vehicles) looks at how to design electric motors so that permanent magnets can be easily removed and the rare-earth metals can be recycled. Some car makers, such as Volvo, are also testing new ownership models, like “Care by Volvo”, where customers lease cars directly from the company instead of buying them. The logistics industry is very important in the Netherlands because the country is in a key transit location where goods move every day. The Netherlands is an example of an EU country that is shifting towards a circular economy because its economy depends strongly on imported raw materials (for example from China). This dependence makes the country vulnerable to changing and sometimes unpredictable import costs for these primary goods. Research on the Dutch logistics industry shows that about 25% of Dutch companies know about and are interested in the circular economy. For larger companies with more than 500 employees, this rises to 57%. Sectors such as chemical industries, wholesale trade, industry, and agriculture, forestry and fisheries see potential cost savings when they reuse, recycle, and reduce imports of raw materials. Logistics companies can support a circular economy by: helping customers reduce costs through better shipment and route planning offering take-back services for used products and packaging Moving from one-way (linear) packaging flows to circular flows (where packaging is reused or recycled) is critical for the sustainable performance and image of the packaging industry. The Dutch government has a national program to move towards a fully circular economy by 2050. Global freight transport is expected to grow in the coming years. This will increase environmental impacts and the global warming potential of transport, creating new challenges for the logistics sector. The Dutch Council for the Environment and Infrastructure (Rli) has suggested a new framework where logistics companies can create value in different ways across the Dutch economy. Examples include: exchanging resources such as waste or water flows between industries moving from a “transit port” model to a “transit hub” model, where more value is added through services and smart connections The Rli studied the potential role of the logistics industry in three sectors: agriculture and food, chemical industries, and high-tech industries. Circular economy models are widely used in agriculture. Agriculture is essential for global food security and can help reduce climate change. In a circular agricultural system, resources such as water, nutrients, and organic matter are reused as much as possible. However, there are also possible risks for human health and the environment if contaminants remain in recycled water or organic material. These risks can be reduced by working on three main areas, which will always depend on local conditions: improving collection, transport, and treatment of waste and water updating regulations and policy to manage risks The Netherlands wants to have a fully circular economy by 2050. As part of this, it plans a shift to “circular agriculture”. The goal is to have “sustainable and strong agriculture” by around 2030. closing the feed–manure cycle (fodder-manure cycle) reusing as many waste streams as possible (a team “Reststromen” will coordinate this) reducing the use of artificial fertilizers and using more natural manure allowing farms in special “experimental areas” to deviate from certain laws and regulations to test circular practices using common and uniform methods to measure soil quality giving farmers the option to sign agreements with Staatsbosbeheer (the state forest service) so their leased land can be used for natuurinclusieve landbouw (“nature-inclusive management”) supporting initiatives that can increase farmers’ income In the furniture industry, most products are passive, long-lasting items. For this reason, strategies that extend product life—such as repair and remanufacturing—usually have lower environmental impacts and lower costs. Some companies, such as GGMS, support a circular approach by refurbishing and reupholstering furniture so it can be reused instead of thrown away. The EU sees large potential for circularity in the furniture sector. Out of about 10,000,000 tonnes of furniture thrown away annually in the EU, most is sent to landfills or incinerated. By moving to a circular model by 2030, the EU could increase Gross Value Added by about €4.9 billion and create an estimated 163,300 jobs. A study on Danish furniture companies shows: 44% of companies offer maintenance as part of their business model 56% design furniture so it can be recycled The authors concluded that while circular furniture models in Denmark are growing, many companies still lack knowledge about how to make the transition, and changing their business model is often seen as a major barrier. A report from the UK also sees a large potential for furniture reuse and recycling. It found that about 42% of bulky waste sent to landfills each year (1.6 million tonnes) is furniture, and that 80% of raw material used in the production phase becomes waste. Between 2020 and about 2050, around 600 oil and gas installations will have to be decommissioned in the UK sector of the North Sea alone. Over the next decade, about 840,000 tonnes of materials will need to be recovered, at an estimated cost of £25 billion. In 2017, North Sea oil and gas decommissioning became a net cost to the public, with UK taxpayers paying 50–70% of the total bill. Because public money is involved, there is interest in finding decommissioning solutions that are best not only economically, but also socially and environmentally. Organizations such as Zero Waste Scotland have carried out studies to identify parts and equipment that could be reused. Equipment might continue its life in other industries or be redeployed in the oil and gas sector itself. Oil and gas are not compatible with the idea of a truly circular economy, because they are finite resources and their use does not “meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs”. A sustainable circular economy can only be powered by renewable energy sources such as wind, solar, hydropower, and geothermal energy. Many entities today aim for “net zero” carbon emissions. This means they still use fossil fuels but offset some of their emissions by removing carbon from the atmosphere. While this is an important first step, some experts, such as smart grid technologist Steve Hoy, argue that a truly circular economy needs “true zero” instead of “net zero”. “True zero” means eliminating fossil fuel use completely and producing all energy from renewable sources. The renewable energy industry itself is growing quickly. Building and maintaining renewable systems requires energy and raw materials. Even so, because fossil fuel power plants emit so much CO2, the total carbon footprint of renewable technologies over their whole life cycle is much lower than that of fossil fuel generation. However, many renewable systems are still designed and built in a linear way. For a fully circular economy, issues such as design for recycling, reuse of materials, and long-term resource availability must also be considered. In 2018, The Ellen MacArthur Foundation (EMF) identified 138 institutions worldwide that offered circular economy courses. Since then, circular economy topics have been added more and more to teaching programs, with plans for adoption at university, city, and even national levels. Zero Waste Scotland is an example of a nationwide program that aims to include circular economy topics in the Scottish education system. Their “YES Circular Economy Challenge” promotes the idea that every learning environment should have a “whole-environment approach” to learning for sustainability. This means the approach should be strong, visible, assessed, and supported by leadership at every level. A 2021 EMF report compared circular economy course offerings in London and New York. It found that there is not yet a full “whole-environment” coverage of circular economy topics. About 90% of the 80 courses analyzed covered some part of the technical cycle (materials, products, technologies), while about 50% covered some part of the biological cycle (food, biomass, ecosystems). The EMF looks critically at how circular economy courses are distributed.

Ciro Pessoa Mendes Corrêa (June 12, 1957 – May 5, 2020), also known by his Dharma name Tenzin Chöpel, was a Brazilian singer-songwriter, guitarist, and poet. He was known as one of the founding members of the influential rock band Titãs and for his later work with post-punk/gothic rock band Cabine C. He was born in São Paulo, São Paulo. Pessoa, who had cancer, died of COVID-19 in São Paulo on May 5, 2020 at the age of 62.

Emily "Cissy" Houston (née Drinkard; September 30, 1933 – October 7, 2024) was an American soul and gospel singer. After a successful career singing backup for such artists as Roy Hamilton, Dionne Warwick (her niece), Elvis Presley, Aretha Franklin, and Chaka Khan, Houston embarked on a solo career, winning two Grammy Awards for her work. Houston was the mother of singer and actress Whitney Houston, the aunt of singers Dionne Warwick and Dee Dee Warwick, and a cousin of opera singer Leontyne Price. Houston was the grandmother of Whitney Houston's only child, Bobbi Kristina Brown. Houston died on October 7, 2024 under hospice care in Newark, New Jersey from problems caused by Alzheimer's disease at the age of 91.

Ahmet Civan Canova (28 June 1955 – 20 August 2022) was a Turkish actor, playwright and theatre director. He was born in Ankara, Turkey. His career began in 1974. He was known for his role in the 2006 movie Home Coming as Iskenceci Komiser. He also was known for his role in the Netflix series The Gift as Mustafa Özgürsoy. Canova died of lung cancer on 20 August 2022 in Istanbul, Turkey at the age of 67.

Ciwan Haco (born 1957) is a Kurdish singer. He was born in the city of Qamishli in northern Syria near the border with Turkey. After finishing high school, he left for Germany in order to continue his studies. He studied music at the University of Bochum for three years. After university, he started his career as a singer. He combined Kurdish folk music with western style pop music, rock, blues, and jazz. He has released 14 albums. He become well known on the Kurdish music scene after he sang for more than 200.000 people in Batman, south Turkey, in 2003. Haco lives in Sweden with his wife. He has two children, Lorin, 7, and Rosa, 5.

Claes-Göran Hederström, (20 October 1945 – 8 November 2022) was a Swedish singer. He made his musical debut at SVT in 1967. He represented Sweden in the Eurovision Song Contest 1968 with the song Det börjar verka kärlek, banne mej. The song ended up coming 5th. Hederström died on 8 November 2022, at the age of 77.

Claes-Johan Rudolf Andersson (30 May 1937 – 24 July 2019) was a Finland-Swedish psychiatrist, author, poet, jazz musician and politician. He was born in Helsinki. He was a member of the Finnish Parliament, representing the Left Alliance and the Finnish People's Democratic League. He was member of Finnish Parliament in 1987–1999 and 2007–2008. Andersson died at a hospital in Helsinki from problems caused by a long-illness on 24 July 2019 at the age of 82.

Claire Chazal (born 1956) is a French journalist, novelist and former French news director for the TV channel TF1. From 1991, Chazal was the presenter of TF1's weekend news until the last broadcast on 13 September 2015. Anne-Claire Coudray, who had often substituted for Chazal when she was absent, was her replacement. Between 2010 and 2015, after the news, she also presented the program Reportages at 1:30 p.m. Chazal hosted Je/nous de Claire, a talk show on the gay TV channel Pink TV that he helped start in 2004. The title of this show plays phonetically on the title of the French film Le Genou de Claire. Chazal graduated from HEC Paris. She holds the equivalent of a doctorate in economics.

Claire Catherine Danes (born April 12, 1979) is an American actress. She was born in New York City, New York. Danes starred as Angela Chase in My So-Called Life in the 1994-1995 television season. She also acted in many movies, including the 1996 movie Romeo + Juliet, the 2007 movie Stardust, and the 2010 movie Temple Grandin. She plays Carrie Mathison in Homeland. Danes was married to Hugh Dancy, they have three children together, first son born in 2012, second son born in 2018, and first daughter born in 2023.

Dorothy Arlene "Claire" Dodd (December 29, 1911 – November 23, 1973) was an American actress. She acted in several movies. She played secretary Della Street in The Case of the Curious Bride and The Case of the Velvet Claws. Dodd was born in central Iowa. She died from cancer in Beverly Hills, California.

Claire Windsor (14 April 1892 – 24 October 1972) was an American actress who acted primarily in movies in the silent era. Her career lasted close to 27 years, although she made many very notable movies in her career. Windsor was born in Marvin, Kansas. She died of a heart attack in Los Angeles, California at age 80.

Claire Elizabeth Foy (born 16 April 1984) is an English actress. She played Anna in the 2011 movie Season of the Witch. She played Kate in the NBC series Crossbones. Foy is known for playing Elizabeth II in the Netflix series The Crown. Foy was born in Stockport, Greater Manchester, England. She grew up in Manchester, Leeds and Buckinghamshire.

Claire Rhiannon Holt (born 11 June 1988) is an Australian actress who acts in both movies and television. She was born in Gold Coast, Australia. She is known for playing Emma Gilbert in H2O: Just Add Water and for playing Rebekah Mikaelson in both The Vampire Diaries and The Originals. Holt was married to American film producer Matt Kaplan in 2016, then in 2017 they ended up divorced. Holt got married again, her second husband named Andrew Joblon, they have three children together, first son born in 2019, first daughter born in 2020 and second son born in 2023.

Jayne Claire King (born Jayne Claire Seed; 10 January 1962) is an English actress. She is best known for portraying the roles of Kim Tate in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale (1989–1999, 2018–present), and Karen Betts in the ITV prison drama series Bad Girls (2000–2004). King also appeared in the fourth series of Strictly Come Dancing (2006), Safari School (2007), and Celebrity Big Brother 14 (2014). Then from 2014 to 2017, she portrayed Erica Holroyd in the ITV soap opera Coronation Street.

Claire Nouvian (born 19 March 1974) is a French environmental activist, journalist, television producer, and film director. Claire Nouvian was born in Bordeaux. She worked in journalism. After that, she worked to protect the ocean and marine life. She was awarded the in 2012. She won the Goldman Environment Prize in 2018. She was the second French person to win this prize (after biologist Christine Jean in 1992).

Claire Elizabeth Cottrill (born August 18, 1998), known professionally as Clairo, is an American singer-songwriter. She started posting music on the internet when she was thirteen. Clairo became well-known when the music video for her lo-fi song "Pretty Girl" was very successful in 2017. She signed a record deal and released her debut EP Diary 001 (2018) with Fader Label. Fader Label was created by her father's friend. Her debut studio album Immunity (2019) had the singles "Bags" and "Sofia". "Sofia" became her first single to chart on the Billboard Hot 100. Her second studio album, Sling, was released in 2021 and was successful. It debuted in the top 20 of the US Billboard 200. Her third studio album, Charm, was self-released on July 12, 2024. Charm received a Grammy nomination for Best Alternative Music Album.

Clarence James "Clancy" Brown III (born January 5, 1959) is an American actor. He is known for his roles as Byron Hadley in The Shawshank Redemption and Career Sergeant Zim in Starship Troopers. He is perhaps best known for his role as the Kurgan in the cult classic Highlander. Brown also works extensively as a voice actor in animated TV series. He was the voice of Lex Luthor on Superman: The Animated Series and Justice League/Justice League Unlimited. He also voices Mr. Krabs on SpongeBob SquarePants.

Clara Schumann (born Leipzig 13 September, 1819; died Frankfurt am Main 20 May, 1896), was the wife of composer Robert Schumann. She was a famous pianist and composer. Clara was born Clara Wieck. Her father taught her the piano and music theory. She was a prodigy and by the time she was thirteen her father was taking her on concert tours. She was only nine years old when Robert Schumann came to Leipzig to study law at the university. Robert Schumann’s family had told him that he had to study law, but he wanted to be a musician. He took piano lessons from Clara’s father, Friedrich Wieck. Clara not only learned the piano, she also studied singing, the violin, instrumentation, score reading, counterpoint and composition. By 1835 she was famous in the whole of Europe and was admired by Goethe, Mendelssohn, Chopin, Paganini and, of course, Robert Schumann. Clara’s father did not want them to marry. He did everything he could to stop the marriage. For several years life was very difficult for them, but in the end, by 1840, they were married.they married by court permission They had a happy marriage and had eight children. Clara played her husband’s piano works (Schumann had a hand injury and had to stop playing the piano). She ran the household and earned money by teaching and performing. Life was not always easy. When they went on tours together Clara was more famous than her husband, and this was difficult for him. Robert often had depression. They both taught at the Leipzig Conservatorium and Clara also taught privately in Dresden and Düsseldorf. Robert Schumann died in 1856 after two years in a mental asylum. Clara was left with seven small children to bring up. Nevertheless, she continued her career as a pianist and often travelled to other countries, especially England, where she played Robert’s piano works. She was great friends with Brahms and often performed his works, too. Clara’s own compositions are all from her early years. She was a very gifted composer. In those days people thought that women should not be composers. Playing the piano was one thing, but a woman was not expected to be a professional composer. Clara knew this, and devoted more time to her playing, and to editing her husband’s music. Clara’s compositions include more than 20 piano works, a piano concerto, some chamber music and several songs.

Clara Gordon Bow (; July 29, 1905 – September 27, 1965) was an American actress. She was born in Brooklyn, New York City. She was one of the most famous movie actresses in the history of silent movies. Bow died September 27, 1965 of a heart attack in Los Angeles, California at the age of 60. Bow acted in 57 movies between 1922 and 1933. She is considered the first American sex symbol after her work in the 1927 movie It. That movie also created the term "The It Girl" meaning the most popular girl at the moment. Bow was the original It girl. She was the person every movie studio tried to get in their movies. She was the person who the audiences always want to see more of. She was the focus of media attention. She retired at age 28. In 1944 Bow tried to kill herself. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia. Bow was born in Prospect Heights.

Clara Blandick (June 4, 1876 - April 15, 1962) was an American actress. She acted in stage plays and movies. She played Auntie Em in the movie The Wizard of Oz. She also did many other movies. She was raised in Boston. She moved to New York City for her acting career. Blandick committed suicide at age 85 using sleeping pills.

Clare Victoria Balding (born 29 January 1971) is a British television presenter. She was born in Kingsclere, Hampshire. She is openly lesbian. In 2009, she was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. She recovered later that year. In 2012, a book she wrote about her life was published. It was called My Animals and Other Family. In February 2013, Woman's Hour, a programme on BBC Radio 4, put her on their list of the most powerful women in the UK. Balding presented Britain's Brightest in 2013.

Clare Cathcart (3 October 1965 – 4 September 2014) was a Northern Irish actress. She appeared in the television series New Tricks, Call the Midwife and Doctors. She also appeared in Holby City, Father Ted and The Bill. Cathcart was born in Bellanaleck, County Fermanagh. Cathcart died from an asthma attack on 4 September 2014 in Brighton, East Sussex. She was 48.

Clare Tree Major (1880 - October 10, 1954) was an English American actress, author, and stage director. She started the Children's Theatre of New York in 1924. She was born in 1880 in England. She migrated to the United States in 1914. In 1924 she started the Children's Theatre of New York. In 1925 she produced the play The Little Poor Man. She died on October 10, 1954.

Cologira "Clara" Cannucciari (née Bonfanti; August 18, 1915 – November 29, 2013) was an American YouTuber. She hosted the web series Great Depression Cooking with Clara and wrote the book Clara's Kitchen. Clara Cannucciari was born in Melrose Park, Illinois on August 18, 1915. Her parents, Giuseppe and Giuseppina Bonfanti, had recently moved from Sicily. The family was very poor during the Great Depression. Because of this, her mother helped the family save money. From 2007 to 2011, she made her mother's meals for the web series Great Depression Cooking with Clara. Her grandson Christopher made the series. The last episode, Tomato Sauce, was posted on December 24, 2011. Unreleased episodes have been shared over time. On March 25, 2020, Christopher announced he would start posting more videos of her onto their YouTube channel. Clara Cannucciari died on November 29, 2013, when she was 98 years old. Her daughter-in-law, four grandchildren and three great-grandchildren were still alive. Her son, Carl, died in 1992, when he was 42 years old.

Clare Camille Johnson (born August 23, 1979), known professionally as Clare Grant is an American actress, model and producer. She co-founded Team Unicorn. With Team Unicorn, Grant has produced several web series and music video parodies. These include "Geek and Gamer Girls" and "All About That Base".

Clare Margaret Holman is an English actress. She played forensic pathologist Laura Hobson in the crime drama series Inspector Morse and its spin-off Lewis from 1995 to 2015. Clare Margaret Holman was born in London, England. Holman started her acting career in the 1988 television film The Rainbow. In 1989 she played a school teacher called Mary Llewellyn in an adaptation of The Fifteen Streets by Catherine Cookson. In 1991, she played Iris Bentley in the film Let Him Have It, and in 1992, she voiced Juliet in the Shakespeare: The Animated Tales adaptation of Romeo and Juliet. She played Harper in the Royal National Theatre's production of Tony Kushner's Angels in America in November 1993. In 1995, she played Laura Hobson in the crime drama series Inspector Morse. Holman was nominated for a 1997 Laurence Olivier Theatre Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role in 1996 for her performance in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?. She was in three episodes of Midsomer Murders as three different characters. The episodes are called Country Matters (2005), Ring Out Your Dead (2002), and The Miniature Murders (2019). In 2006, Holman replayed her role of Dr Hobson in the series Lewis. In 2007, Holman played Wendy in the television series Fallen Angel. She portrayed Anglo-Irish noblewoman Mabel Bagenal in Brian Friel's play Making History. In October 2013 she played Liz in the Tricycle Theatre production of the Moira Buffini play Handbagged, and in 2015, Holman was in the film Suite Francaise. From April to May 2015, she played Myra Bolton in Doris Lessing's play, Each His Own Wilderness, at the Orange Tree Theatre in Richmond, London. Holman has directed six episodes of Doctors in 2010 and two episodes of Holby City in 2012. Holman was married to Howard Davies. They married in April 2005 in Stratton, Cornwall, and were together until his death in October 2016. She has stepchildren and stepgrandchildren from her husband's previous marriage. She supports ending violence against girls, contributing to Plan UK, part of the world's biggest campaign for girls' rights.

Clarence Clemons (January 11, 1942 – June 18, 2011) was an American musician and actor. He as known on stage as the Big Man. He died in his Florida home after having a large stroke. He was born in Norfolk, Virginia in 1942. His father gave him an alto saxophone for Christmas one year. Clemons' saxophone playing was an important part of early songs by Bruce Springsteen, including "Rosalita" and "Born to Run". Clemons released his for solo album in 1983.

Clarence Williams III (August 21, 1939 – June 4, 2021) was an American actor. He was best known for his role as "Linc Hayes" on the iconic "hippie" cop show The Mod Squad (1968-1973). He was nominated for a Tony Award. His last movie role was in the 2013 movie The Butler. Williams III was born on August 21, 1939 in New York City. He died of colon cancer on June 4, 2021 in Los Angeles, aged 81.
Clarence Charles "Ducky" Nash (December 7, 1904 – February 20, 1985) was an American voice actor. He was the voice for Disney cartoon character Donald Duck for almost 50 years.

Clarence Alexander Avant (February 25, 1931 – August 13, 2023) was an American music executive, entrepreneur, and movie producer. He was sometimes known as the "Godfather of Black Music". He was born in Climax, North Carolina. He founded Sussex Records on December 18, 1969. In October 2016, Avant received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Avant died at his home in Los Angeles, California on August 13, 2023 at the age of 92.
Clarence Marion Kelley (October 24, 1911August 5, 1997) was an American politician. He was the second Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation from 1973 to 1978.

Clarence "Skip" Ellis (May 11, 1943 – May 17, 2014) was an American computer scientist, and Emeritus Professor of Computer Science and Cognitive Science at the University of Colorado at Boulder. While at the CU-Boulder, he was the director of the Collaboration Technology Research Group and a member of the Institute of Cognitive Science. Ellis was the first African-American to earn a PhD in Computer Science (1969), and the first African-American to be elected a Fellow of the ACM (1997). Ellis was a pioneer in Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) and Groupware. He and his team at Xerox PARC created OfficeTalk, one of the first groupware systems. Ellis also pioneered Operational Transformation, which is a set of techniques that enables real-time collaborative editing of documents.

Vithana Kuruppu Arachchilage Clarence Arthur Somasinghe Wijewardena JP (,; 3 August 1943 – 13 December 1996), known professionally as Clarence Wijewardena, was a Sri Lankan singer, composer, and musician. He is considered one of the most respected musicians in Sri Lanka. Wijewardena made a big change to Sri Lankan Sinhala pop music by using an electric guitar in Sinhala music in the 1960s. Because of his influence on Sinhala pop music, he is often named the "father of Sri Lankan pop music".

Clarence Darnell Gilyard Jr. (December 24, 1955 – November 28, 2022) was an American actor. He was best known for his roles as private investigator Conrad McMasters on the legal drama series Matlock (1986–95) and Texas Ranger Jimmy Trivette on Walker, Texas Ranger (1993–2001). He also played Theo in the action movie Die Hard. Gilyard died at his home in Las Vegas, Nevada on November 28, 2022 from a long-illness at the age of 66.

Clarence George Carter (January 14, 1936 – May 13, 2026) was an American singer-songwriter, musician and record producer. His best known songs were "Slip Away", "Back Door Santa" (both released 1968), "Patches" (1970) and "Strokin'" (1986). Carter died on May 13, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia from pneumonia caused by prostate cancer and sepsis at the age of 90.

William Clark Gable (February 1, 1901 – November 16, 1960) was an American actor. He was best known for playing Rhett Butler in the 1939 movie version of Gone with the Wind. Gable was born on February 1, 1901 in Cadiz, Ohio. He was married five times. He had two children. The last movie that Gable starred in was The Misfits, in 1961. This movie also starred Marilyn Monroe and was written by Arthur Miller. Gable died shortly afterwards in Los Angeles, California, after having had a fourth coronary thrombosis. Gable was nominated for an Academy Award for playing Fletcher Christian in the 1935 movie version of Mutiny on the Bounty. A year before in 1934, he starred in It Happened One Night with Claudette Colbert. Their performances won them both an Academy Award (the only wins in their careers).

Clarice Taylor (September 20, 1917 – May 30, 2011) was an American stage, movie and television actress. She was known for her television role as Anna Huxtable in The Cosby Show. She died from heart failure, aged 93.

Robert Clark Gregg (born April 2, 1962) is an American director, screenwriter, actor and voice artist. He has acted in both television and movies. Gregg is known for his role as Phil Coulson in Iron Man, Iron Man 2, Thor, and The Avengers. Gregg was born in Boston, Massachusetts. Gregg married Jennifer Grey in 2001. They have a daughter, Stella Gregg. They divorced in 2021.

Clark James Gable (September 20, 1988 – February 22, 2019), also known as Clark Gable III, was an American actor, model, and television presenter. He was born in Malibu, California. Gable was a past host of the television reality show Cheaters from the 13th to the 15th seasons. His grandfather was actor Clark Gable. Gable was found dead on February 22, 2019 in Dallas, Texas of an accidental fentanyl overdose, aged 30.

Clark Tinsley Middleton (1957 – October 4, 2020) was an American actor. He was best known for his roles in Kill Bill: Vol. 2, Sin City, Fringe, Snowpiercer, and The Blacklist. He was born in California. Middleton died on October 4, 2020 from the West Nile virus in Los Angeles, aged 63.

Clarke Timothy Gayford (born 24 October 1976) is a New Zealand radio and television broadcaster. He was a presenter of the fishing documentary show Fish of the Day. He is the husband of former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern.
Claron McFadden (born 1961) is an American soprano singer. She became known because she sang in the opera Lulu by Alban Berg, at Glyndebourne Festival Opera.

Claude Kiambe (born 16 September 2003), known professionally as Claude, is a Congolese-born Dutch singer and songwriter. He represented the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025 with the song "". In 2019, Claude took part in the eighth season of The Voice Kids, he made it through to the battle stage of the competition but was eliminated. His debut studio album, Parler français, was released on 15 November 2024 and peaked at number six on the Dutch Albums Chart. The album includes the singles "Ladada (Mon dernier mot)", "Layla (Take Me on Your Way)", "Vas-y (Ga maar)", "Écoutez-moi", "Parler français", "La pression" and "Je t'aime". On 19 December 2024, AVROTROS the Dutch broadcaster announced that Claude would be representing the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025. His song "", was released on 27 February 2025. On 17 May 2025, he finished 12th in the Grand Final.

Achille-Claude Debussy (born Saint-Germain-en-Laye, France, 22 August 1862; died Paris, France, 25 March, 1918) was a French composer who was one of the most important composers of the early 20th century. Most of his compositions are for orchestra or for piano. He also wrote some songs, chamber music and one opera. He made his music very different from the Romantic style, which other composers used at the time. He is called an Impressionistic composer {citation needed: by who?} because he was influenced by the group of painters called the "Impressionists". They were less interested in making their paintings look exactly like the real world but preferred to paint things such as the effect of the sunlight shining on water. Debussy often did so in his music, which creates a special atmosphere. Claude's father was a travelling salesman, and his mother worked as a seamstress. He learned the piano when he was young and joined into the Conservatoire de Paris at the age of 11. He did not do well enough in his examination to qualify as a concert pianist. After winning the Prix de Rome, he went to Rome for two years. He visited Bayreuth in 1888 and 1889 to hear Richard Wagner’s operas. He preferred sounds of the Javanese gamelan, which he heard in Paris at the World Exhibition. In 1899, he married Rosalie Texier. He was also employed as music critic of a journal called La revue blanche, and wrote his opera Pélleas et Mélisande, which was performed at the Opéra-Comique. The opera was performed 100 times there during the next ten years. He wrote for orchestra--Fêtes galantes and a work called La Mer (The Sea)--which he wrote while he lived in Brighton, England. Debussy was starting to become very famous. His personal life changed. He left his wife because he had fallen in love with Emma Bardac who was an amateur singer for whom Gabriel Fauré had written a song cycle: La Bonne Chanson. Her husband was a banker. Bardac bought an apartment, where Debussy lived with her for the rest of his life. They had a daughter, called Chou-Chou, who was born in 1905. They married in 1908. Debussy’s next orchestral work was called Images. He began composing a set of preludes for piano. Other works followed: Khamma, Le martyre de St Sébastian and the ballet Jeux, which was produced in 1913 by Segei Dyagilev’s company. People soon forgot about that work because only two weeks later, the same ballet company produced Igor Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring, which caused a riot. By this time Debussy was ill with colorectal cancer. His visit to London in 1914 was his last trip to another country. He wrote more piano works: a set of Études and a piano duet called En blanc et noir (In White and Black). He planned to write six sonatas, each for a different group of instruments, but he only wrote three of them: one for cello and piano, one for flute, viola and harp and one for violin and piano. The Sonata for violin and piano (1917) was the last work that he played in public; he played the piano. He died of colorectal cancer in 1918. Camille Saint-Saëns, for example, did not understand the way that Debussy's musical ideas flowed gently into one another. He was always an opponent of Debussy. There is a lot of variety in Debussy’s piano music. Some of it is difficult to play like the Études and pieces such as L’isle joyeuse (The Happy Island). Other collections are much simpler like Suite bergamasque, which includes the very popular piece Clair de lune (Moonlight). He wrote two books of preludes. Each of the pieces has a title, but it is printed at the end of each piece, as if he did not want the listener to know what it was about until afterwards. Debussy wrote wonderfully for the voice, making the music just right for the rhythm of French. That can be heard in his songs and his opera. Using melodies and harmonies which are often quite simple he creates a special kind of dream-world which can be very powerful. He often uses the whole-tone scale and the pentatonic scale which give the music a hazy feeling because it does not seem to be clearly in one particular key. He liked to use unusual chords for their own sake, not for them to lead to a particular key. He also used old scales known as the church modes. Debussy’s music had a great influence on many 20th-century composers. John Cage, Olivier Messiaen, Pierre Boulez, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Frederico Mompou all learned from listening to his music.

Claude Marion Akins was an American actor (born May 25, 1926, in Nelson, Georgia - died January 27, 1994, in Altadena, California). With his big body and deep voice, Akins usually played the clever (or less than clever) tough guy, on the side of good or bad, in movies and television. He is famous as Sheriff Lobo in the 1970s TV series B.J. and the Bear, and later The Misadventures of Sheriff Lobo, a spinoff series.

Claude Jarman Jr. (September 27, 1934 – January 12, 2025) was an American actor. A child actor, he was known for his roles in Rio Grande starring alongside John Wayne and Maureen O'Hara and in High Barbaree. He was nominated for an Academy Award in 1946. His final movie role was in Disney's The Great Locomotive Chase (1956). Jarman died at his home in Kentfield, California, on January 12, 2025, at the age of 90.

Claude Marcelle Jorré, better known as Claude Jade (; 8 October 1948 – 1 December 2006) was a French actress. She was known for starring as Christine in François Truffaut's three movie Stolen Kisses (1968), Bed and Board (1970) and Love on the Run (1979). Jade was born in Dijon, France. Jade died on 1 December 2006 in Boulogne-Billancourt, France of uveal melanoma and liver disease at the age of 58. Claude Jade studied acting at the State Conservatory in Dijon. She was already acting in television series in Paris when she was discovered at the theatre by François Truffaut: She played the leading role in his film Stolen kisses (1968). A year later, she played Alfred Hitchcock's American film Topaz. One of her most successful roles was in 1969 as Manette alongside Jacques Brel in Mon oncle Benjamin by Édouard Molinaro. Claude Jade continued to act in films by François Truffaut (Bed and Board, Love on the Run) and achieved great popularity as the heroine of the series The Island of 30 Coffins (1979). Claude Jade has worked internationally in the US, Japan, the Soviet Union, Italy, Belgium and Germany. She has appeared in 80 cinema and television productions. She also continued to act in the theatre. Her last role was Célimène in the play Célimène et le cardinal in 2006.

Claude Evrard (29 July 1933 – 20 April 2020) was a French actor. He was born in Versailles, France. His best known roles were in Circus Angel, Le Distrait and If the Sun Never Returns. His last movie role was in the 2017 drama Back to Burgundy. He also starred in the 1990s television series Les Cinq Dernières Minutes. Evrard died on 20 April 2020 in Clamart, France at the age of 86.

Claude Heater (October 25, 1927 – May 28, 2020) was an American opera singer and actor. He was also known for playing the role of Jesus Christ in the 1959 classic movie Ben-Hur. Heater was born in Oakland, California. Heater died on May 28, 2020 from heart disease in San Francisco at the age of 92.

Claude B. Klee (born 1931, died April 3, 2017) was an French biochemist. She was awarded a 1991 Presidential Executive Rank Award. In 1992, she was elected to the National Academy of Medicine. She graduated from the University of Marseille. She studied with M. Staehelin. She worked with Herbert Tabor, Louis Sokoloff, and Maxine Singer. She worked at the National Cancer Institute. Claude Brasseur (15 June 1936 – 22 December 2020) was a French actor. From the late 1950s until two years before his death, Brasseur appeared in 150 movies and television productions. He was known for his role as Arthur in Jean-Luc Godard's Bande à part (1964). Brasseur played the lead role in the early 1970s historical crime television series The New Adventures of Vidocq. Brasseur died on 22 December 2020 in Paris, at the age of 84.

Claude Bolling (10 April 1930 – 29 December 2020) was a French jazz pianist, composer, arranger, and actor. He was born in Cannes, France. He was known as the composer of the Lucky Luke animated movies Daisy Town (1971) and La Ballade des Dalton (1978). Bolling died on 29 December 2020 in Saint-Cloud, France at the age of 90.

Claude Kahn (9 November 1935 – 17 November 2023) was a French classical pianist, internationally known for his interpretations of especially the music of Chopin, but also of French music (Debussy, Fauré, Ravel) as soloist or accompanied by great orchestras in the world. He founded and directed a piano competition in 1970, to become international as the Concours International de Piano Claude Kahn. He founded the conservatoire of Antibes in 1971 and directed it until 1991. He died in 17 November 2023, eight days after his 88th birthday.

Émilie Chauchoin (; September 13, 1903July 30, 1996), professionally known as Claudette Colbert was an American actress. Colbert was famous for her comedy and drama. She became one of the biggest box-office stars of her time. In 1999, she was ranked as the 12th greatest female star of all time by the American Film Institute in their list AFI's 100 Years... 100 Stars. Colbert once said to an interviewer, "Audiences always sound like they're glad to see me, and I'm damned glad to see them." Claudette Colbert was born Emilie Chauchoin on September 13, 1903 in Saint-Mandé, France. Her parents were Georges Chauchoin and his wife, the former Jeanne Loew. Her family emigrated to the United States and settled in New York City. She had one brother, Charles, who used the surname Wendling and went on to become his sister's agent. After her formal education ended, she enrolled in the Art Students League, where she paid for her dramatic training by working in a dress shop. She made her Broadway debut in 1923 in the stage production of "The Wild Wescotts". It was during this event that she adopted the name Claudette Colbert. One of the brightest film stars to grace the screen was born Emilie Claudette Chauchoin on September 13, 1903, in Saint Mandé, France where her father owned a bakery at 57, rue de la République (now Avenue Général de Gaulle). The family moved to the United States when she was three years old. She began acting in high school. In 1923, she was on Broadway for a small part. She loved the role and gave up on her plans to be a fashion designer to instead have a career in acting. She made her first movie appearance in 1927, in For the Love of Mike. This was a silent movie. It was shot in Paramount Studios in New York, New York facilities. However, sound movies (also called "talkies") were becoming popular. 2 years later, Colbert was in her first talking movie, The Hole in the Wall This movie co-starred another newer actor, Edward G. Robinson. In 1930 Colbert signed a contract with Paramount Pictures. At the time, they were looking for stage actors who could do dialog in the new "talkies". Colbert had a very elegant and musical voice. Therefore, she was very important to companies like Paramount. Some of her early hit movies were Manslaughter (1930) and Honor Among Lovers (1931), both with Fredric March, The Smiling Lieutenant (1931), with Maurice Chevalier and Miriam Hopkins, and Torch Singer (1933), with Ricardo Cortez and David Manners. Colbert's career got a huge boost when Cecil B. DeMille cast her as the Roman empress Poppaea in his historical epic The Sign of the Cross (1932), opposite Fredric March and Charles Laughton (as Nero). In one of the most memorable scenes in movie history, Claudette bathes nude in a marble pool filled with asses' milk. She worked again for DeMille and was dazzling as his Cleopatra (1934), opposite Warren William and Henry Wilcoxon. In 1934 she won an Academy Award for Best Actress for her role opposite Clark Gable in the Frank Capra classic screwball comedy It Happened One Night, a movie she initially described as the "worst picture in the world". Her performance, however, proved to Hollywood that she was an expert comedienne. She initially balked at pulling up her skirt to entice a passing car to give her and Gable a ride in one famous scene, complaining that it was unladylike. However, upon seeing the chorus girl who was brought in as her body double, an outraged Colbert told the director, "Get her out of here. I'll do it. That's not my leg!" Colbert then starred in the original Imitation of Life (1934), opposite Warren William and Louise Beavers. Claudette spent the rest of the 1930s deftly alternating between romantic comedies and dramas, and found success in both: Private Worlds (1935), with Charles Boyer; She Married Her Boss (1935), with Melvyn Douglas; The Gilded Lily (1935) and The Bride Comes Home (1935), both with Fred MacMurray; Under Two Flags (1936), with Ronald Colman; Tovarich (1937), again with Boyer; Bluebeard's Eighth Wife (1938), with Gary Cooper; Zaza (1939), with Herbert Marshall; Midnight (1939), with Don Ameche; It's a Wonderful World (1939), with James Stewart; and Drums Along the Mohawk (1939), with Henry Fonda. In addition to Capra and DeMille, Colbert was working with the top directors in the industry: Dorothy Arzner, Ernst Lubitsch, Preston Sturges, Frank Lloyd, John M. Stahl, Wesley Ruggles, Gregory La Cava, Anatole Litvak, George Cukor, Mitchell Leisen, and John Ford. Colbert believed that her face was difficult to light and photograph, and was obsessed with not showing her "bad" side, the right, to the camera, because of a small bump that resulted from a childhood broken nose. From 1936 to 1944, she starred in numerous programs of Cecil B. DeMille's Lux Radio Theater, which was one of the most popular dramatic radio shows at the time. In 1952, she returned to work in her native France where she stayed until 1955. Apart from making two more Hollywood movies, she went back to Broadway in 1958 doing "The Marriage Go-Round" with Charles Boyer, earning a 1959 Tony Award nomination for her work. Also for her Chicago theatre work, in 1980 she won the Sarah Siddons Award. In 1984 she appeared with Rex Harrison in Frederick Lonsdale's "Aren't We All" at the Haymarket Theatre, London, and also the Brooks Atkinson Theatre on Broadway, presented by Douglas Urbanski. Ms. Colbert's last movie was Parrish in 1961. She acted in numerous Broadway plays for the next twenty years. Her final appearance before the cameras was in 1987. She did a television mini-series titled The Two Mrs. Grenvilles. She was nominated for an Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Mini-series or a Special. In 1988, she won the Golden Globe Award for Best Performance by an Actress in a Supporting Role in a Series, Mini-Series or Motion Picture made for TV. In 1989 she received the Kennedy Center Honors. During her career, Claudette Colbert played in sixty-five movies. For her contribution to the motion picture industry, she was honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. She did, however, remain on the stage where she had returned in 1956, her first love. After a series of strokes, Claudette divided her time between New York and Barbados. On July 30, 1996, Claudette Colbert died in Speightstown, Barbados. She was 92 years old. Colbert married twice. Her first husband was Norman Foster, an actor and later a director, whom she married in 1928 and divorced in Mexico in 1935. According to the account of the divorce in the New York Times, published on August 31, 1935, "Some secrecy surrounded the proceedings, for while Mr. Feldman [Colbert's agent] apparently was at liberty to tell of the divorce being granted, he said he could not tell where in Mexico it was obtained." The report further stated that "The Fosters created something of a sensation when they disclosed that they were trying to remain happily married while living in separate homes. But even this experiment apparently failed." Four months after her divorce, on December 24, 1935, Colbert married Dr. Joel J. Pressman, a throat specialist, who died in 1968; her former husband went on to marry the actress Sally Blane, a sister of Loretta Young. When she retired from motion pictures, Colbert and her husband moved to Palm Springs where she operated a store for a time before moving to Barbados. The idea of moving to Barbados came to her following a visit to Noël Coward's house in Jamaica. At her home there, called Bellerive, she spent her later years as a hostess to the world's powerful and famous. Ronald Reagan was one of her guests during his presidency, as were Lillian Helman, Kirk Douglas, Jack Benny, Rex Harrison, and Slim Keith. She had a small guest house built on the property for the honeymoon of Frank Sinatra and Mia Farrow. Colbert died at her home in Barbados, following series of small strokes during the last two years of her life at the age of 92, and she was interred there in the Parish of St. Peter Cemetery along with her mother and husband. A requiem mass was held at St. Vincent Ferrer church in New York City later. According to an article published in August 10, 1996 issue of the Cincinnati Post, the childless Colbert left most of her estate, estimated at $3.5 million and including her Manhattan apartment and her home in Barbados, to a friend, Helen O'Hagan, a retired director of corporate relations at Saks Fifth Avenue, whom Colbert had met in 1961 on the set of Parrish, the actress's last movie. Bellerive was later bought by David Geffen. After Colbert's death, rumors about the actress's purported lesbian relationships, including supposed affairs with Marlene Dietrich and Greta Garbo, began to circulate in the international media. In response, Colbert's friend Helen O'Hagan told the New York Daily News that the actress barely knew Dietrich or Garbo and that Colbert was "a man's lady". The purported Colbert-Dietrich relationship also was explored in the 2001 book Behind the Screen: How Gays and Lesbians Shaped Hollywood, 1910-1969 by William J. Mann, a movie historian.
